look_here_first: LOOK HERE FIRST: check a leafy flowering stem, NOT flower color alone. (1) The UPPER stem leaves are ALTERNATE with broadened bases usually clasping to AURICULATE-CLASPING (small ear-like lobes wrapped around the stem). (2) Lower leaves may be relatively broad, unevenly crenate/serrate or lobed; basal foliage sometimes persists but may wither. (3) Stems often have longer spreading hairs lower down, becoming more appressed upward. (4) Small showy heads with exceptionally MANY thin white or pinkish ray florets (FNA 150–250, occasionally up to 400) around a yellow disc; involucre about 4–6 mm high. For comparison, E. strigosus typically has narrower, NONCLASPING upper leaves and often fewer (~50–100) rays; E. canadensis bears many much smaller inconspicuously-rayed heads. Confirm using leaf insertion and fresh head, not pink versus white alone.

morphology_keys.life_cycle: Annual, biennial or short-lived perennial, 4–80 cm typical; fibrous rooted with a simple crown (FNA). Root structure cannot be verified from the existing main gallery.
morphology_keys.stems: Erect, leafy, often spreading-hairy toward base (hirsute-villous), upper parts more sparsely hairy/appressed. May be minutely glandular; inspect with hand lens rather than inferring hair angles from a flower-only picture.
morphology_keys.leaf_arrangement: Basal and alternate cauline (stem) leaves; lower leaves often obovate to oblanceolate, 3–11 cm usually, sometimes larger. Lower edges scalloped (crenate), sharply toothed (serrate), or even lobed.
morphology_keys.leaf_attachment: Stem leaf bases typically CLASPING to AURICULATE-CLASPING, meaning a broadened base and small ear-shaped lobes wrapping partly around the stem; high-value separator from usually nonclasping E. strigosus. In current leafy linked source the meeting point is visible, but whether fully clasped is partially obscured by overlap.
morphology_keys.leaf_hairs: Basal leaves sparsely to densely hairy, upper leaves variably hairy; stem hairs can spread lower down. Hair directions vary along the stem, so never assert all hair is spreading.
morphology_keys.flowerheads: (1–)3–35 heads usually arranged in a rather loose flattish-topped cluster near upper stem. Each head has 150–250 (rarely up to 400) very slender white or pale pink rays, each about 5–10 mm long, surrounding yellow central disc florets.
morphology_keys.involucre: Green cup of overlapping phyllaries under head; FNA dimensions 4–6 mm high by 6–15 mm across. Existing backlit side-source shows outline; no mm reference in photo.
morphology_keys.fruit: Small one-seeded cypsela ~0.6–1.1 mm, with distinct outer pappus setae and inner 15–20 (occasionally to 30) bristles. No fruit macro measured or arrows installed.
morphology_keys.ecology: Occurs in moist to moderately disturbed meadows, roadsides, open lawns and riparian margins; local native-zone certification intentionally not assessed in this finished-card pass.
morphology_keys.variation: White, pale lavender, and pink rays occur; near-white flowering plants can still be this species. Leaf-base and stem/flower characters in combination matter more than rays' tint.

comparisons.key_distinctions: With actual flowers: Philadelphia fleabane usually combines abundant fine rays (FNA 150–250[–400]) and CLASPING/AURICULATE upper stem leaf bases. Prairie fleabane E. strigosus often has NONCLASPING narrow upper leaves and fewer rays (commonly 50–100); overlap/variation require multiple features. Horseweed E. canadensis bears scores of much smaller pale greenish heads, with fresh rays inconspicuous. E. annuus is a showy white-rayed look-alike but is often coarser-leaved; inspect FNA key. E. tenuis may have subclasping leaves, so clasping alone isn't a 100% separator.

field_key.check: Photograph actual upper leaf base and head at matched scale, do not use color alone.

photo_diagnostic_lesson.title: Philadelphia fleabane — find the leaf 'ears', then inspect its fine rays

steps.look: Leafy flowering stems and lower leaves
steps.text: Photograph whole plant with base and stem branches. Old foliage may persist or wither; don't force a rosette-only ID.

Follow an upper leaf to where it wraps partly around the stem. This 'ear-lobed' AURICULATE-CLASPING feature is the critical photo role. The linked leaf picture shows an attachment but does not conclusively resolve the entire wrap.
Using a hand lens, check whether lower stem is spreading-hairy, and upper stem more appressed or sparsely hairy. Short plant photos usually can't certify tiny hairs.

steps.look: Hundreds of fine pale rays and a yellow disc
steps.text: Unlike horseweed's tiny nearly rayless-looking heads, Philadelphia fleabane shows many fine white to pink rays (150–250 usually). Pink alone is not diagnostic.
Turn the flower head sideways to locate green involucre / phyllary cup below rays, and distinguish unopened rounded buds from pappus fruit. Use ruler to measure involucre height.
Ripe one-seeded fruits need a 1 mm macro to distinguish outer setae and inner bristles. No photo installed that resolves this.

glossary.auriculate: With small ear-shaped lobes at the base of a leaf.
glossary.clasping: Leaf base partly wrapping the stem instead of simply tapering to a narrow connection.
glossary.cauline: Growing on the upright stem rather than around the ground-level crown.
glossary.crenate: Leaf edge with rounded scallop-like teeth.
glossary.hirsute: Covered in coarse or fairly long hairs.
glossary.ray_floret: Narrow strap-shaped outer floret that looks like a petal.
glossary.disc_floret: One of the many tiny tubular flowers making the yellow center.
glossary.involucre: Green cup of bracts supporting a daisy-like flowering head.
glossary.phyllary: One bract in the green cup under the head.
glossary.pappus: Fine hairs/bristles helping the mature one-seeded fruit travel by air.

photo_diagnostic_lesson.memory_rule: CLASPING little leaf-ears + lots of fine pale RAYS + hairy leafy stem = Philadelphia fleabane candidate. Prairie fleabane: usually nonclasping; horseweed: barely obvious tiny heads.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Philadelphia fleabane — find the leaf ears
steps: START with the new USGS picture: find the leaf BASE where its broad tissue partly CLASPS the green hairy stem; contrast PRAIRIE fleabane's usual narrow nonclasping base.
Look at a genuinely fresh composite head; Philadelphia often has 150–250 or more fine white/pink ray FLORETS around a yellow central disc. Color alone is not a diagnosis.
Turn the flower head over for its green involucre and inspect lower stem hair direction; check a real plant's leaf node from multiple angles.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: A verified partly clasping upper leaf base (now in USGS photo) plus fine many-rayed heads supports Philadelphia fleabane. Stem hairs and basal foliage are supporting; exact Texas county nativity not reviewed.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: USGS photograph shows the place to look and visible partial clasping; it does not show fully encircling leaf ears or 1mm cypsela traits. Public-domain license is guide-specific and credited.
